MorphoHand · real_v1 fingertip and screwdriver, two-pad rig · contact comparison bed · 5 October 2026 · built 2026-10-07 15:13

Agreement and cost of five fingertip contact models on pinch, twist, roll, shake and brake tasks

The 1 mm sphere pad spins the screwdriver at 6 % less torque than Drake hydroelastic from 0.5 to 3 N, slips at the same pull force, rolls the tool as Drake does and brakes the swing to within 1° of Drake. Over the nine metrics of the agreement table its median deviation from Drake is 6.2 % in MuJoCo, 6.0 % in MuJoCo-Warp and 6.2 % in Newton; condim 4 gives 5.7 % with a single contact point, Newton’s mass-corrected hydroelastic tip 19.3 % and point contact, which transmits no torque, 95 %. The pad’s largest stable step follows in 19 of 21 settings. A pad step costs 15 µs on one CPU core against 1,298 µs for Drake, and 1.08 µs per world-step in a MuJoCo-Warp batch on one GPU (1.19 in Newton). Under a held load at half the slip force every MuJoCo model creeps (slides slowly) 150–260× faster than Drake, and Newton’s hydroelastic tip 25–50×.

Terms and metrics

pad
One fingertip’s contact with the tool. On the bed rig two pads, one per fingertip, pinch the tool; is the normal force of each pad.
friction arm
Pressure-weighted mean distance of the contact patch from its centre, (1), in mm. A pad transmits at most about its normal before it spins. The hydroelastic law (3), integrated over the screwdriver patch, gives 0.82, 0.97 and 1.28 mm at 0.5, 1 and 3 N.
slip onset, effective
Task 1 raises an axial force on the tool at 2 N/s. Before onset the tool slides slowly at a speed proportional to the force; onset is the force at which the speed leaves that trend. Effective is the onset force divided by (two pads). Rigid Coulomb friction gives 1.000.
creep
Steady sliding of the tool while the load stays below the slip force. Task 1 holds the axial force at half the onset force for 1 s and reports the sliding speed in µm/s; task 2 holds half the onset torque and reports the turning speed in °/s; in task 4 it is the drift per cycle below the Coulomb threshold. Rigid Coulomb friction gives zero.
slip speed
Mean sliding speed of the tool over the 50 ms after onset in task 1, in mm/s. Rigid Coulomb friction with equal static and kinetic gives 34 mm/s.
arm at spin onset
Task 2 raises a torque about the pinch axis; the onset torque divided by , in mm per pad. Sliding arm: the steady torque while the tool is driven to spin at 1 rad/s, divided by . Onset / law: onset torque over the hydroelastic law’s . Onset torque on its own is the torque at spin onset, in mN m; Drake gives 0.84, 1.97 and 7.65 mN m at 0.5, 1 and 3 N.
drift per cycle
Net displacement of the tool along its axis per 5 Hz shake cycle in task 4. Coulomb load ratio: ; rigid Coulomb friction slips above 1.
swing end, largest swing, peak rate
Task 5 lowers the pinch force from 6 to 0.2 N over 4 s, with the tool’s centre of mass 15 mm off the pinch line, until the tool swings about the pinch axis. Swing end is the final angle (90° = hanging), largest swing the largest angle over the run (Drake: 87.3°), peak rate the largest angular speed of the swing, in °/s.
rolling ratio
Task 3 moves one pad 10 mm along the tool’s surface at 10 or 50 mm/s while both pads press at , so the tool rolls between them. The rolling ratio is the tool’s rotation times its radius over half the pad travel. Rolling without slip gives 1 between flat pads and 1.008 between the two spheres, whose line of centres tilts as the pad moves; a contact point inside the tool surface rolls on a smaller radius and raises it. Slip: the path length of the relative motion of tool and pad at the contact point over the travel, in µm.
physics step
The simulator’s integration step; 1 ms unless stated. µs per step: wall time of one physics step on one CPU core, controller and rendering excluded. World-steps per second: on the GPU, the number of parallel simulations times the steps each completes per second; µs per world-step is its inverse.
, ,
MuJoCo contact parameters. , the solref time constant, sets how fast a penetration is corrected; , the solimp impedance, sets what fraction of that correction the solver enforces; is MuJoCo’s estimate of the contact’s inverse inertia (47.2 kg for a pad on the real tool). Together they set the sphere stiffness, (10).
inverse weight , effective mass
is MuJoCo’s body_invweight0 of body , its translational inverse inertia at the reference pose in 1/kg; for a contact between bodies 1 and 2, and .
,
Newton’s per-shape hydroelastic stiffness (pressure per unit depth, for a layer of modulus and thickness , in N/m³) and its friction gain, which SolverMuJoCo turns into the friction-row time constant of each contact.
impratio, condim
impratio: ratio of friction-row to normal-row stiffness in MuJoCo; larger values make friction stick harder. condim 3: normal force and two friction directions; condim 4 adds torsional friction about the normal.
pad spacing
Distance between neighbouring sphere centres on a sphere pad. The 2, 1 and 0.5 mm pads have 51, 205 and 819 spheres on a 45° cap.
relaxation time
Drake’s dissipation time for hydroelastic contact, 10 ms on the bed. A pad sphere’s equivalent is , (10): 20 ms for the 1 mm pad and 30 ms for the 0.5 mm pad.

Rig, models and protocol

Every case runs on the two-pad pinch rig of the 10-01 study (scripts/hom_contact_rig.py): two real_v1 fingertip spheres on rails along x press the screwdriver, whose axis lies along y, with a commanded force N per pad. Tasks add one load or motion each. The protocol (docs/experiments/20261005-contact_bed/PROTOCOL.md) fixes the parameters, metrics and row fields for every script, so rows written by different scripts and simulators compare directly. 759 rows so far. Table: task 2 at a 1 ms step. The law is the hydroelastic pressure field integrated over this rig’s sphere–cylinder patch, 0.974 mm·N−1/4 (scripts/hydroelastic_arm_integral.py). Point contact has no torsional friction; its onset value is the torque at which its creep reached the detection speed.

Newton hydroelastic with starts to spin at 2.4–2.6× the law’s torque. SolverMuJoCo writes each hydroelastic contact’s stiffness as a solref time constant, which MuJoCo turns into a force stiffness multiplied by the contact’s effective mass; dividing by the pad–tool effective mass of the solver’s own model (17.4 g) gives 0.77–0.88× the law, with no fitted parameter (overview, step 7; rows ../20261006-newton_mass_scaling/).

Task 3: roll between the pads

Protocol: gravity off; after the pinch settles at N per pad, the +x pad moves 10 mm along z (across the tool axis) at 10 mm/s for 1 s, or 50 mm/s for 0.2 s, driven by a stiff servo on a 100 kg slide, while both pads stay force-controlled at N along x; then a 0.2 s hold. The tool rolls between the pads. Rows: roll.jsonl (scripts/contact_bed_roll.py) and ../20261006-simulator_agreement/roll_newton.jsonl (scripts/contact_bed_newton.py roll).

Table: task 3 at a 1 ms step and 10 mm/s. Rolling ratio: tool rotation times its radius over half the pad travel. No-slip ratio at the contact point: the ratio for rolling without slip about the force-weighted contact point, which lies inside the tool surface by the contact depth; the line of centres of the two spheres tilts by 12.6° over the travel, so no-slip rolling on the surface gives 1.008. Slip: path length of the relative motion of tool and pad at the contact point. Friction use: tangential over μ times normal force at the moving pad; 1 is sliding.

Every model rolls the tool at 0.5 to 3 N, 10 and 50 mm/s and 1 and 5 ms (88 cases, none lost). The rolling ratio is 0.994–1.001 of each model’s own no-slip value, the contacts slip at most 33 µm over 5 mm of rolling, and the moving pad uses at most 20 % of its friction. The ratios differ between models by where the contact point sits: the deeper the point lies inside the tool, the smaller the radius it rolls on and the larger the ratio. Point contact and condim 4 place it at the deepest penetration point, the pads at the force-weighted centre of their spheres, and Drake and Newton at the centroid of the pressure field.

Task 6: creep, impratio and noslip

Task 6 ran on 2026-10-06 (406 rows in creep.jsonl): the 1 mm pads at relaxation times 0.02, 0.05 and 0.1 s crossed with impratio 100–10 000 and 1–10 noslip_iterations on tasks 1, 2, 4 and 5. Raising impratio from 100 to 1000 cuts the median creep of bed task 6 from 16.8 to 1.0 µm/s; ten noslip_iterations take it to -0.54 µm/s. The analysis is on the fingertip page, docs/experiments/20261006-fingertip_backends/20261006-fingertip_contact_backends.html, artifact.

Task 7: largest stable step

Protocol: the 1 mm pad pinch holds the tool at N = 1 N per pad with gravity on, across the tool axis. Every contact gets solref (, 1) and solimp (, , 0.001, 0.5, 2). Each step runs a 0.4 s settle with the weight compensated and a 1 s hold without it; a case holds when the state stays finite, the tool centre stays within 5 mm and both pads keep a contact. Every pair runs with MuJoCo’s clamp off, which tests the bound, and on, as MuJoCo runs by default.

Bed task 7 holds the tool against gravity at 1 N per pad for 1 s with from 0.2 to 0.95, of 5, 10 and 20 ms and steps from 0.25 to 15 ms, with MuJoCo’s clamp switched off so that stays as set. For 19 of the 21 pairs the largest step that held and the first that failed bracket (14) (Figure 4). In the other 2,  = 0.9 and 0.95 at  = 20 ms, the tool is ejected at 15 ms, below bounds of 18–19 ms. Point contact, one row per pad, fails at 3, 7 and 10 ms for 0.2, 0.5 and 0.9 at  = 10 ms, the first tested steps above , where (14) with  = 1 gives  = 10 ms. With the clamp on, as MuJoCo runs by default, the pads with  ≥ 0.5 hold at every step up to 10 ms at all three , and those with 0.2 and 0.35 fail from 2 to 10 ms, where the clamped bound falls below .

Consistency of the pads

The 1 mm pad gives the same task results from 0.5 to 5 ms steps: the arm at onset moves by under 1 % and the swing end by under 0.1°. The 0.5 mm pad agrees with it; the 2 mm pad touches with too few spheres at 0.5 N, and its arm there is less than half the law’s.

The bed rig steps MuJoCo-Warp as a CUDA graph and Newton without one, so its GPU column compares the rigs. The SR2 holding fixture of the batched sweep captures every 10-step block as a CUDA graph in both simulators; its one-world column compares the simulators.

What this does not settle

  • Friction rows of Newton’s hydroelastic contact. Its friction gain gives the friction rows a 3.9 ms time constant where the pads use 10 ms. Repeat task 5 with contact_bed_newton.py brake --models newton_hydro_mc at for 2, 5, 10 and 20 ms; a swing within 3° of Drake’s at one setting would make the remaining creep and swing differences a friction-row setting.
  • Creep against Drake. Every MuJoCo model creeps 150–260× faster than Drake under a held load (task 1). Task 6 lowers it with impratio and noslip_iterations; the next measurement is the chain’s hold and wield at impratio 1000, which decides whether creep matters at the task level.
  • Largest steps of the stability map. At  = 20 ms and 0.9 and 0.95 the tool is ejected at 15 ms, below the bound of 18–19 ms. Run contact_bed_stability.py --d0 0.9 0.95 --tc 20 --dt 11 12 13 14 --refsafe 0 to locate the failing step and compare it with the numerical bound (15–16 ms).
  • One GPU world. The bed’s Newton rig steps one world from the host without a CUDA graph (2.0–2.8 ms per step) where the MuJoCo-Warp rig captures one (0.27 ms). Capturing Newton’s step in the rig would give its one-world cost without the launch overhead.
